\begin{proof}
Define
\[
\mathcal{T}=\bigcap_\alpha\mathcal{T}_\alpha.
\]
Because each $\mathcal{T}_\alpha$ is a topology on $X$, the intersection contains $\varnothing$ and $X$. If $\{U_i\}_{i\in I}\subseteq\mathcal{T}$, then every $U_i$ belongs to every $\mathcal{T}_\alpha$, so $\bigcup_{i\in I}U_i$ belongs to every $\mathcal{T}_\alpha$ and hence to $\mathcal{T}$. Similarly, finite intersections of members of $\mathcal{T}$ belong to $\mathcal{T}$. Therefore $\mathcal{T}$ is a topology on $X$.

By its definition, $\mathcal{T}\subseteq\mathcal{T}_\alpha$ for every $\alpha$. Conversely, any topology $\mathcal{O}$ on $X$ contained in every $\mathcal{T}_\alpha$ satisfies $\mathcal{O}\subseteq\mathcal{T}$. Hence $\mathcal{T}$ is the largest such topology, and therefore it is unique.
\end{proof}

Let
\[
\mathcal{T}=\bigcap_\alpha\mathcal{T}_\alpha.
\]
For every $\alpha$, $\mathcal{T}_\alpha$ contains $\varnothing$ and $X$, so these sets belong to $\mathcal{T}$. If a collection of sets is contained in $\mathcal{T}$, then it is contained in every $\mathcal{T}_\alpha$; consequently, its arbitrary union belongs to every $\mathcal{T}_\alpha$ and hence to $\mathcal{T}$. The same argument for two, or finitely many, sets shows that $\mathcal{T}$ is closed under finite intersections. Thus $\mathcal{T}$ is a topology on $X$.

The intersection definition gives $\mathcal{T}\subseteq\mathcal{T}_\alpha$ for all $\alpha$. If $\mathcal{O}$ is any topology on $X$ contained in every $\mathcal{T}_\alpha$, then each member of $\mathcal{O}$ belongs to their intersection, so $\mathcal{O}\subseteq\mathcal{T}$. Hence $\mathcal{T}$ is the largest topology on $X$ contained in all the collections $\mathcal{T}_\alpha$. Since a largest topology is necessarily unique, the result follows.
\end{proof}
